utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good afternoon to you Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. So everyone is present from the accused. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey. Defence team, same situation, same situation as yesterday. I couldn't see you behind the pillar, behind the column, Mr. Vanderpuye. My apologies to you. Right. Let's finish with Mr. Haynes' cross-examination. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Yesterday evening, just before we broke, we were looking at a notebook or a note you had written of an intercept at 8.28 in the morning of the 15th of July of 1995; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you remember that you were good enough to confirm for me from the text of that intercept three or four details about it. The first was that one of the collocutors, to use your word, was X or Jocic and that man was looking to get in touch with somebody called Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't have the intercept in front of me, but I assume that it is as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it's perfectly simple. If you want to confirm it, it's P1170A, and we can have it put up in front of you. And, Witness, you take all the time you want to consider your note, but what I was asking you to confirm was your note revealed that one of the speakers was X or Jocic, and he was looking to get in touch with somebody called Obrenovic. Would you confirm that that is something you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this. As for the collocutor X, this may be Jocic, but at the moment I was noting it down I wasn't sure of his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the second thing you told me about yesterday was that X asked to speak to called to somebody called Travera Peru after which a third speaker appeared to whom you assigned the initial P.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the person to whom you assigned the initial P, said that he was in contact with Obrenovic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the last thing which we dealt with before we broke was that X or Jocic said that Vinko had been asked to go over to his men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it too well on the screen, but it is more or less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It needs to go down a line or two for you to be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what you told me at the very close of yesterday evening was that you couldn't remember whether you asked for this particular radio conversation to be treated as urgent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just one or two other things about that before we move on. The channel that you were monitoring when you listened to this conversation was channel 3, wasn't it? If you want, we can bring the document down a bit so you can see the top.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If it says channel 3, that was the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And channel 3 was generally found between 784.6 and 784.7 megahertz, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer remember that. I don't remember the exact frequencies, but I presume it can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we won't go through a whole series of them to show you that, I'm sure we can agree that. At the time you recorded this conversation did the name Obrenovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking I knew very little about the individuals whose conversations I was surveilling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But in particular, and I know it's a long time ago, do you recall whether the name Obrenovic was of significance at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking about it today I can remember, or rather I cannot remember anything to do with that last name at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about the name Vinko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was better known, he was a brigade commander, so it was a rather well-known first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to move on now to the next intercept in the sequence, which is behind our tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for the witness, can we please have P1171B on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While that is being done, have you updated the -- where is it? Sorry for the interruption, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Mr. President, absolutely not. Can we go to the bottom of the page, please, on this exhibit? A bit further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the first thing we notice about this particular intercept is it's not recorded on a pre-set channel, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation was picked up by another type of device.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. And 255.850, that's the frequency on which it was recorded, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I think it is an RR-1 device.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I suggested to you a little while ago that channel 3 was in the region of 784 megahertz, 255 megahertz is quite a long way around the dial from that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not absolutely certain as to the gist of your question, but when we have a mention of channels it is one type of device, whereas when we have frequencies mentioned it is a different type of device, and they use different antenna -- antennas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of the frequency, 255 megahertz, is that likely to be a different sort of communication from something transmitted at 784 megahertz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication principle is the same, but RR-1 uses one channel, and the RR-800 has about 20 channels in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you, I'm not going to press this too far. But looking at that entry below 255.850 at 8.34, all the writing there is your writing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of doubt, this is six minutes after the last intercept we were looking at that ended with the X saying that Vinko was going to be sent to his men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have all of it in front of me, all I can see is the message we discussed a bit ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what you see there to the bottom of the page is all that there is to this message, and what you've written down is 10 to 12 words, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, that's the entire message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But I think you agree that's a summary of a very -- longer conversation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a possibility of that, but I cannot recall the exact duration of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and help you remember it, to see if you can help us as to how long that conversation was and what it contained. You've written at the top of there that there were two collocutors, X and Jevtovic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: X Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry that's my pronunciation, but yes, X Jevdjevic. Is it the case that the conversation was sufficiently long for you to identify Jevdjevic as a speaker in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what is written down, it is clear that Jevdjevic was identified. As to how, I don't know. Whether he introduced himself or whether the conversation was long, I can't tell you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was Jevdjevic's voice one which you would have instantly recognised or would you have needed the context to identify him as a speaker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember who Mr. Jevdjevic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So you would accept it is more likely that you identified him as a speaker from the context of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One possibility is to use the context, the entire conversation, and another possibility is perhaps that someone on the switchboard asked for a particular person. Several options are possible, and I don't know which one was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful of you. Do you recall whether this short 10 or 12-word summary was a summary of one conversation or a series of conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the details, I can only assume that this concerns one conversation and that this was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and help you a little more. I'm going to remind you of something you said when you made a witness statement in 1999 and I'm going to ask, please, that you are shown P02337 at page 3 of the English and page 4 in the B/C/S. We need to go forward one page in the B/C/S, please. Now, can you look at the second paragraph down from the top in the B/C/S version and read it over to yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, I've already read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is what's written there correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you can see that the conversation you -- you showed to the investigator was page 45 of book 1 which was the very conversation we've been looking at. Is it right therefore that during the course of this conversation some attempts were made to find Vinko Pandurevic but he couldn't be found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation or the information conveyed is as it stands. I don't know what else is behind it. I just conveyed what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm just intrigued about what you said in May of 1999 when you made a witness statement, because you said you remember a conversation "when our commander Semso Muminovic was requesting a meeting to see Vinko Pandurevic but he couldn't be contacted." Were attempts to contact Vinko Pandurevic made during the conversation we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Muminovic asked to speak with Mr. Pandurevic, and it was an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Muminovic ask to speak to anybody else during the course of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you now, please, to be shown 4D60 at page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the number? 4D60?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 4D60. Could the English version be pulled down a little further, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you read that, Witness? Or is it too small for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want you to look at the subparagraph 2, towards the bottom of the page, please. I asked you some questions about this. This is an occasion when you met with Stefanie Frease and some other people about 11 days after you made your witness statement. And again you recalled conversations that you had heard and, at number 2, you said one was about opening a corridor. "It was a call made by one of our commanders, Semso Muminovic, in which he was looking for Furcula." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly. I cannot recall this particular detail and who it was that Semso asked to speak to. This is the statement I gave, and there is such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So there is a possibility, is there, that the 10 or 12 words you wrote down reflect the whole series of conversations in which Semso Muminovic was looking for Furcula and Vinko Pandurevic and attempts were made to contact Vinko Pandurevic, which all came to nothing. That's what these 10 or 12 words actually represent, a whole series of conversations like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a possibility, although I am uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Can we go back briefly, please, to P1171B? Thank you very much. Bottom of the page again. Now, there's a word there in square brackets that's got lines drawn around it. That means urgent, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you wrote the word "urgent" on that message, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was it about the fact that Semso Muminovic wanted to talk to Vinko Pandurevic that was urgent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was urgent because it concerned Srebrenica. People were trying to break through the lines and it was an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, you can't tell all that from that message, but that was what you knew it was about, was it? You knew it was about a corridor and people getting through the lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I evaluated that there was a possibility of the corridor being closed, but I wasn't really -- that it would be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the other detail about that message I want to ask you a couple of questions about was, you managed to record the frequency on which Semso Muminovic was going to contact Vinko Pandurevic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this was -- this was very important, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very important, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you monitor that frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this particular type of frequency being monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I want you to help me about this. Here you've got a very important message where one of your commanders is trying to make contact with a brigade commander from the Bosnian Serb army and you've got the frequency on which they were going to talk to one another. What orders were you given about monitoring any conversations on that frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no order, simply it was -- this was an ultrahigh frequency and we were also monitoring reserve connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But as you told me at the very start of this cross-examination, what conversations you monitored and recorded were substantially your -- in your discretion. Why didn't you monitor this frequency after that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was on the zones that would be monitored. This frequency I don't think was supposed to be monitored by our sector. It was to be monitored by the brigade sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you aware whether the brigade sector was given an order to monitor this frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just want to clear up one point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, was -- the frequencies you were listening to, was that up to your discretion or did you receive orders on which frequencies to listen to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received the zones that we were supposed to monitor conversations in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Down at the bottom of this, is that an FR before the number 144, and so on, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says F2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what that -- I mean you wrote that. Do you know what that means, F2 or FR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been some sort of channel on the small radio station device.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that number 144 -- what is that number, can you tell me that? I won't try to guess.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the frequencies used by people who have powerful radio stations and these are not relay connections. These are direct connections that don't need relay stations in order to work. These stations are used by the police service, the fire service, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just -- just so the record is clear, can you tell us what numbers and/or letters are written there, those six digits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So witness, that brings us to the end of the questions. On behalf of the Tribunal I like to thank you for your testimony. Our staff will assist you for your return back home. On behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, I think we can start with the tendering process. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe you may have this sheet, and we have the -- the under seal pseudonym sheet PO2337, and then we have the series of intercepts -- sorry, that's the 92 ter statement, 2337. The pseudonym sheet is 2338. And then all those intercepts you see have their own numbers which I think we can hopefully count on the document that you have, as well as there's notebooks noted at the end and those are all the things I have made reference to and as we know the process is, I would just have them marked for identification until we get to the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Am I to take it that the ones in bold are being tendered to remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. Ms. Stewart has just reminded me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You have been given a copy of this, the various Defence teams? I am, of course, safeguarding what we have agreed upon in the past already in relation to your general objection on intercepts and also on the notebooks. Are there any objections? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a problem with P2341, because if this intercept was, in fact, written down by the witness that we heard, it's the same conversation that was also in the Prosecution's motion of the 15th of December and you rendered a decision on that decision. In that decision of the 15th of December, the Prosecutor was stating that this particular conversation was intercepted by the witness PW-137. So I am not able to say who, in fact, intercepted this conversation and this is why I would like the Prosecutor to state clearly who was the operator who intercepted that particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. McCloskey, second page, bottom. PO2341.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure what counsel's referring to, but I can look into that. But I can tell you this -- this: As we've established, this witness did review the handwritten notebook and did identify his handwriting. And so I believe the foundation has been laid, and if someone else did this intercept as well, that's possible, or if we've got our intercepts mixed up, that's possible as well. I will check into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A point of clarification. This is the conversation number 8 which was annexed to the motion of the Prosecutor, and the Prosecutor himself identified the operator as being PW-137. Now this conversation was identified by the witness during the meeting that they had with the Prosecutor. It is possible that this conversation, however, may have placed by mistake in -- in this bundle. Maybe that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you consider it necessary and if the witness is still here, we could ask him in again. Show him the intercept and he will confirm whether this is his handwriting or not. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see if he's still in the building. Madam usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we have that notebook, sometimes they are with other witnesses, but we'll try to take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In relation to witness PW-137, it is the person we have decided will be made available for cross-examination if any of the Defence teams will notify us within seven days earlier of the need to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we bring him in, we might want to just find the notebook. There are many of them. Or we can all wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are still -- we can still operate under the same conditions as before, namely with voice distortion. I just want a confirmation on that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And this is a notebook readily available here, or do you have to bring it over from somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a pretty good collection. Whenever I look for notebooks, it's always the last one in the box, but I think Ms. Stewart has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it on the ELMO so that the Defence has an opportunity to -- no, but I want to see it myself, and I want to make sure that we have the same -- he's being shown the same document. It's Madam Fauveau in particular. I mean of course I'm not excluding any of the other Defence teams, but ... All right. The ERN number should be, Madam -- 667, 666. Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe the ERN should be -- 0080-0666 is the beginning of the intercept, and if we could place it on the ELMO, and I -- I guess I should just ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just put the question, Mr. McCloskey. Further examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, what we've asked you to come back in for is if you could just take a look at this notebook and at this intercept that it's -- that it's open to. Make sure I've got the right part. It begins -- it's 1802 hours. And please take a look at the original -- the original notebook, if you could. Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you wish to put any question, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I just wanted to inform you that the Defence of General Miletic will not request that the witness PW-137 be called back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Witness, I thank you once more. We needed to clear that up. You will now be escorted by our usher. And have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So these documents will be admitted with the -- or marked for identification with -- according to the usual practice that we have been following, both as regards the intercepts and as regards the notebook. The pseudonym sheet of course is admitted and will remain under seal. The same as regards the witness statement of the 5th of May, 1999. And all those other documents tendered which appear in bold in the list submitted by the Prosecution will, until we decide finally and definitively on whether they are fully admitted or not, remain under seal. Defence exhibits. Mr. Zivanovic, I suppose, goes first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have given our list of exhibits that we used during the cross-examination. It's been given, presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will go through it for the record. It's document 1D127, 1D128, 1D131, 1D140, 1D149, 1D154. These are better described in a sheet of paper that has been submitted by Mr. Zivanovic. However, since on this sheet of paper there is the name of the witness written down, this sheet of paper will be made use of as necessary by the registrar, but will remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to mention that we sent a corrected list and instead of Exhibit 1D131 the Exhibit D126 [as interpreted] has been substituted. We made that correction this morning. Because 1D126 was actually used during the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that correction, Mr. Zivanovic. My recollection also is that all -- yes, exactly. That out of these, 1D127 and 1D128 need to remain under seal. Any objection from any of the Defence teams or from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And of course these, for the time being, will remain marked for identification pending receipt and clearance of the translation thereof. All right? Automatically once the translation comes in and is not contested by anyone, these temporarily admitted documents will become fully-fledged exhibits. 5D.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, document 1D122 is already translated and exists already in the system, and the document 2D45, 2D47, 2D48 will become 5D, with all the other numbers that I mentioned. For those documents I don't have the translation yet. All these documents contain the name of the witness, so I would like to ask that these documents be treated as confidential documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have covered them all. So it's 5D 2D48, 5D122, 5D 2D45, and 5D 2D47, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the first and the last two will be marked for identification for the time being, pending translation. The other one, not hearing any objections, is fully admitted. All right? And all these four documents or exhibits will remain under seal. Now, Mr. Haynes, you did make use of one or two documents. Do you wish to tender them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The witness statement is already in evidence, and I don't wish to tender the small section of the information report that I put to him because it's read into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any other document that any of the Defence teams would like to tender? None. So that closes the chapter as regards this witness, Witness number 69. We are going to raise an issue with you. Which is the result of -- a sense of frustration and also a lot of thought, and in-depth discussion that is we've had amongst ourselves before and after the recess. For quite some time now we have been hearing, receiving the evidence of several intercept operator witnesses. Despite growing concerns on our part, we believe we have been extremely patient and we've shown much judicial restraint up until now and have not intervened in the examination of any of these witnesses. However, as a result, we have had very lengthy evidence, resulting in a considerable amount of time consumed, dealing with repetitive evidence, and evidence which in some instances appears to be of marginal relevance at best. You are, as much as we are, fully aware that there are several other witnesses currently scheduled to appear in this case dealing again with intercepts, about 14 or 16 left. And the Trial Chamber is very concerned that continuing with the current approach will add unduly to the length of this trial with the presentation of evidence that is unnecessarily commutative and of minimal relevance. We have given this a hell of a lot of thought and we have come to the conclusion that the situation is no longer tenable. We are fully aware of our duty to ensure the fair and expeditious conduct of this trial, and we have fully considered what might or could be done with a view to avoiding the continuation of such problems. Before issuing any orders, however, we thought it fit to give you an opportunity to air your views on this, and in fact we are going to give you an opportunity now to make submissions on what you think can be done to expedite this process when dealing with these intercept operator witnesses. We will start with you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As you might imagine, well, we share the same concern because these are very difficult witnesses, with all the material and minutia. We have -- in each of the three trials I've done we have tried to sculpt the intercepts as appropriate to the trial. This based on the judges, based on the case. We have early on received your views about -- about intercepts, especially intercepts relating to acts or conduct of the accused. We have seven accused here. Unlike the other trials intercepts were important but they weren't of this vast number. The -- Krstic had a few very important intercepts. Blagojevic and Jokic had a few, but not many. This case has many, many intercepts that go to the acts or conducts of the accused, which as you know, the Bench has shown have a particular importance. We have chosen our witnesses basically with two criteria, one, supervisor witnesses that can give you the idea of how this programme worked. And that is done not only so you can understand the programme at the two sides and -- with the MUP and with the headquarters, but also the -- all the intercept operators whose intercepts may be important but don't go to acts or conduct, we believe they go to foundation as a quasi-business records. So that's why the supervisors have been chosen, the very few supervisors you have seen. All the other witnesses have been chosen only because we have identified one or more intercept that go to an act or conduct of the accused that we feel is something that is worth you seeing. There are acts or conduct evidence out there that don't amount to the kind of evidence that we think you need to hear. So we have made a judgement on each and every one of these witnesses that there is an important intercept in there that you should see. And I can pick those -- I know you don't want this, but any intercept operator that we choose I will show you why we -- the intercept was important, how we believed it went to acts or conduct, and why we chose it. For example my last witness, I didn't have him go over any intercepts in a sort of an offensive manner, I mean that in a sport sense, to show you a Popovic or a Beara intercept. I just -- he just authenticated his 27, and there are several in there, and that will be dealt with by analysis in a later period. But each witness has an important intercept to the -- that go to the acts or conduct of the accused and we felt we needed that intercept into evidence for your analysis, and I think as you have seen our motions based on your decision that in order for an intercept to be relevant, if it went to acts or conduct you needed to hear from that witness and they needed to cross-examine him. And I think that has been -- borne out to be not a bad decision, because I think we're gaining information from the cross-examination and from the direct that goes to important evidence. I think that was, in retrospect and at the time an important decision according to the law and a decision that I think should stand, as should that -- those future intercepts that go to act or conduct. My instructions to myself and to my counsel are that -- is that the rest of these people are 92 ter, if at all possible, with maybe the exception of the MUP supervisor who -- you have heard there are challenges about the MUP. And we are, if we haven't, we mean to be trying to get every one of these folks as 92 ter, with -- and I have, in looking at their statements, I have he been reading these long transcripts of previous trials that much of it is spent reading in intercepts because that was the process we chose. I have instead, in my last witnesses, chose to take the two or three-page report, which had the guts of what we wanted and their background, and left any examination about intercepts to the direct examination. And that's -- that's -- are my instructions to mitre. Everybody 92 ter, try to keep your summary as -- you know, as short and to the point as possible. I'll leave it to the lawyers if they want to use the trial transcripts, they may. Mr. Thayer is going to be using the trial transcript on another witness. I like to use, if we have a good statement, the statement. And regarding questions on direct under 92 ter, my -- my practice and my instructions reflect what you saw with this last witness. There wasn't a very good record about his -- his previous education and he had no -- he wasn't the HAM radio guy and didn't have much -- didn't have any radio experience, that's why I went into a bit on his engineering background, very, very short. And then pretty much after that I concentrated on individual intercepts and only in situations where I thought that an individual intercept that was important had a bit of information that needed to be clarified, like 01. 01 is code for the commander of a unit, and it can be read either 01 or -- the letters ON, which means "he." So I needed just to bring out through this witness that he couldn't tell whether it was 01 or he, so that if Mr. Butler or someone else is interpreting that he will take that into account and you will understand why he is. The same thing with Jocic. The -- Jocic, I just wanted to clarify that you were aware that that was a three-party intercept and that Jocic meant X, so I took a brief time to do that. That is the kind of thing I wanted to do so we are not left with intercepts that may have importance or do have importance with question marks around it. It is my burden to prove this case beyond a reasonable doubt, this is important evidence, so I chose a few to do that. Certainly that -- this guy had, what, 29 intercepts? I kept a pretty limited group, and I kept my -- the mistakes between the two fairly limited so you could get an example of some of the differentials. But those are my instructions, those are our practices, to 92 ter these folks, do a brief summary, and only ask questions about individual intercepts or particular areas that we think might help the court and we're trying to keep it within a half an hour, whenever we can. That may depend on the particular intercept. As you remember, our first intercept operator had an intercept with several changes he made, so we spent a fair amount of time, as did the Defence. There is one coming up like that that may also take some time. But that's my practice, that's what -- we're trying to keep this as minimum, as short as possible, and we look really forward to the time when we're through with these folks. Now, I also occasionally object when I think something is more time consuming than relevant. We haven't objected much. We think that many times objections can cause more time, and the Court's been handling this very well in my view, so you have noticed we're not taking very many objections, and that is also our strategy. If we can -- if we cannot object, we won't object. And that -- that's our strategy: Get through these witnesses as -- as quickly and as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Incidentally, although you -- or rather we have noted of course what you have said that you have given instructions to your staff that all these witnesses will be 92 ter witnesses, however we still have at least in our records, four of these that have not yet been indicated as such. Three of them had been indicated initially as 92 bis witnesses, and we had denied your request for two of them, namely 78 and 80, because their statements and the intercepts went to the acts and conduct of one or more of the accused. And in relation to another, number 79, we had denied outright as you had not submitted the full transcript of his evidence. So you are being requested to attend to these apart from -- apart from the matters that we -- we are discussing -- we are discussing now. Defence. Who would like to address the Chamber on this? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I'd like to say that with a few to the nature of our Defence case and the fact that we are questioning the authenticity of the intercepts and especially when they are put in a wider context, all I can say is that I try and do my best to shorten my cross-examination and to take as little time as possible to the Chamber. However, one needs to bear in mind that a large number of documents corroborating our assertions is something that we are still finding in the database. Therefore, it is necessary for us to put some of those intercepts before the Prosecution witnesses so as to corroborate the thesis we have, the basis for our case. This is all I needed to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask Mr. Zivanovic one question for clarification. You said you are questioning the authenticity of the intercepts. So take the example of the previous one. The previous witness said when he was called again, he confirmed his handwriting. Are you saying that he was lying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I am merely asserting that he didn't write it down at the time marked. It is our thesis that the handwriting discussed here was not made at the time marked on the page. Otherwise we do not dispute the authenticity of the handwriting itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I now understand your submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would agree with what my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic just said and also on our cross-examinations, it is not the authenticity that is in issue, but the accuracy and the reliability, and what weight, if these intercepts some are all are admitted you should give to each separate intercept is an issue. For example, you may not know that, but the upcoming witness, like Mr. McCloskey stated earlier, there had been an intercept with several changes. The upcoming witness has a page and a half on one intercept that is crossed out and then it's rewritten in, handwritten. I've just been told at 2.15 or 2.14, by my colleague from the Prosecution, Mr. Vanderpuye, that that is being translated into English, it never has been, and he's supposed to have those before -- hopefully before the witness testifies. I think he probably has them now. I think I saw somebody bring Janet in. You may not know, he has also handed all of us documents, four separate ones, which are amendments. For example, amendment to tab 1, amendment to tab 3, which are different English translations of the same alleged intercept. And these are placed in front of us literally minutes before this trial commenced today. So frankly I would agree with Your Honours that I think we would all like to see a less -- less time taken in the cross-examination and/or direct examination. However, our clients have a right to a fair trial, and we always talk about the right to a speedy trial, or a right to a fair trial. In my opinion, I respectfully suggest, Your Honours, that the right to a speedy trial, that issue is no longer in front of this Court. Once this trial commenced, the right to a speedy trial has stopped. Now we want the right to a fair trial. If it takes a little longer then the Prosecutor might envision cross-examination or Your Honours, I would ask you to bear with us. I, for one, and our team, will certainly try to streamline the cross-examination as much as possible. There are problems that crop up and Mr. Vanderpuye will verify what I am saying that there are placed in front of us today, four new translations now, and we're getting a fifth one and I, frankly, wouldn't be prepared to cross-examine him until I am able to look at that. These are just minor details, problems that crop up in this trial, in any trial, I'm not putting any aspersions on anybody. We'll try to do the best that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek don't you think that, for example, your cross-examination of yesterday could have been much shorter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do. I would agree that could be much shorter. The issue yesterday with -- was more of the training because he had no prior training whatsoever. He just had a 30-day course, and I wanted to find out what exactly he did and that sort of thing. And frankly, Judge, yes. And I would also, I don't want to be rhetorical, but I imagine that there's a lot of witnesses in my mind that the Prosecution could have got through a lot shorter than they did also. So, sure, I will take blame that I took a little longer on cross yesterday than I should have. I would like to take a lot less time today but, you see, I won't be able, I don't think, until I see these translations and have time to read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What applies to you, of course, applies to almost everyone else, and also to the Prosecution. We've had additional questions following the summaries which went on to one hour or even more and that shouldn't be the case any longer. We've had very exemplary cross-examinations to the point focusing on the intercepts as well. But what I'm suggesting is the following, and I'm inviting you actually to make submissions on this. Do you think it's the case of hearing more on how many people were at the special -- this facility or in that facility? What machines were used, the system of passing on the handwritten transcript to the encrypting clerk, the number of antennas, the quality of antennas? Do we really need to continue asking questions on this? Haven't we heard enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it please the Court, I'm just looking at what you just said, and I think if you look at my cross-examinations I've never asked any of these intercept witnesses what machines they used, any of those -- quality of the antennas, how many antennas. I don't ask, personally, any of those, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not addressing you at the moment, I am addressing all of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May I sit down then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. What I said is I am inviting you to address this issue because it is on our minds, of course. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to go back to what you pointed out the importance of the equipment and the antenna and this is something I kept insisting on during some of my cross-examination. In consultation with some experts I learned that these are very important issues so as to be able to confirm whether there was a technical possibility to intercept such conversations, having in mind the location of the equipment and where the collocutors were, as well as the radio relay technology and features used in the terrain which was at that time in the hands of the army of Republika Srpska. I insisted on it to some extent, and, by your leave, I intend to continue with that practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, what I said was never meant to diminish the importance of the antenna. What I am suggesting is that isn't it time to realise that the witnesses who could give the information and who actually gave the information have come and gone and that the rest of the witnesses that remain should focus on the various intercepts they are supposed to have, or according to the Prosecution, to have recorded? And this is the whole process, haven't we heard enough about the whole process? Does each and every intercept witness that comes over have to be asked the same questions over and over again, only to have a repetition of how many rooms there were, where the encryption -- encrypting room was, whether the Security Services were in the same building, whether there was interaction? We've been going through the same exercise, the same questions dealing with the same thing, and I don't know. Yes, Mr. -- Are you finished, Mr. Zivanovic? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I for sure understand the concerns of the Trial Chamber with respect to these intercepts and especially what you just mentioned about repetitive questions during cross-examination. Indeed we have been repetitive in asking the same questions over and over to a number of witnesses. But, Mr. President, there is a reason for this. And the reason is that on one hand the Prosecution has been asked to call each and every witness where an intercept goes to the acts and conducts of the accused and once there is a witness here on the stand, I cannot do anything else but to ask those questions that go to the reliability. I don't want to be left at the end of this case arguing, saying that there were 10 intercept operators that came, five said that there were problems, but five didn't say anything as to whether there were problems with the reliability. Looking at the reliability, we and maybe this is something that the Prosecution can stipulate to because we don't know what is the position that the Trial Chamber will take with regards to the reliability. Our point of view is that they are unreliable, that it was a difficult exercise, that they had to be listened to many times, that there was no supervision, that there were problems with voice recognition, that there were problems going from the notebook to the typed version, that there were problems with methodology, about the three dots, about the brackets, about the spaces, about the signatures, about the date. Multiple versions of the same. So all this, Mr. President, I have no choice, but if there is a witness there that can testify on this reliability aspect, we feel that it is our duty to ask those questions to ensure that the record is complete so that at the end when I make my argument I will argue that we believe that these intercepts is an unreliability exercise that cannot be given any weight, should not be even admitted in evidence in the first place. Now, that being said, Mr. President, there are two things I want to address. First is the issue of the -- how important these intercepts are. We have some difficulty because, as stated by the Prosecution, Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. We're getting argument on the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what he has to say first. Let's hear what he has to say first, because it could be related ultimately to the position that we will take eventually. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All I'm saying is that we are told every time we have an intercept operator is that all the intercepts are relevant to all charges and all accused in the indictment. That leaves us no choice. As far as the client that I represent in this case, there are very few intercepts; however, I cannot do anything else with what is said, that all intercepts are all relevant to all accused and all counts, I have no choice but to do the best job I can in order to get this unreliable exercise under way. One of the ways we can shorten this thing is to be more focused on the choice of intercept. Granted this is the choice of the Prosecution, but there is maybe a place where we can do an exercise together and say are all of these intercepts really necessary? And then with respect to -- and that's, of course, I put aside the fact that we have new intercepts being added in the course of the exercise, but that, I have different arguments for this later on. And finally, Mr. President, with regards to the procedure, I suggest two things: First of all is when there is a 92 ter witness that the Prosecution keeps it at introducing the statement without anything else than a summary, and as far as cross-examination is, please, Mr. President, just keep us to not asking at least that we don't have any repetitive questions amongst each other here. If my colleague has asked something about an intercept had to be listened to many times, well, I should not ask that question a second time again. That is an effort we can work on, and we will -- we will absolutely say nothing if you stop us from doing something like that, and we will do the best we can to shorten. But at the same time, the Prosecution can keep it to, this is the statement, this is the summary, let's get on with it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I don't know if I understood you well, but you seem to have entertained the idea at some point in time, that we were hinting that if a witness comes over dealing with intercepts that do not mention your client or make reference to your client, you would not have a right to cross-examine. We never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that if I knew better what the case of the Prosecution was, it would be much better for me to just sit down and not ask any questions. But the fact is, the way things are, I have to consider this as being whatever the Prosecution wants it against my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll give you the floor later. Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm always available to tell him my case, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will try to make myself a little bit more clear in case I haven't been clear enough. Mr. Bourgon is suggesting: Trial Chamber, you can always stop us as we go along and bring us to order, and we will comply. Well, that should be and is always second best. First option, first preference is that you exercise self-discipline, and well I wouldn't like to draw comparisons, but we have had extremely exemplary cross-examinations and we have had cross-examinations that, to say -- to say the least, have been of -- have been frustrating. So this is where we are trying to bring the house to order. We are trying to -- we are asking you to address us, make submissions on how you, yourselves, think - and that includes Prosecution, not just the Defence - think that more self-control and self-discipline can be exercised, particularly in the way of not asking or dealing with areas that have been thoroughly and exhaustively already been covered by previous witness and focus on what is really essential in each and every case of -- each and every witness, and each and every intercept that will be tendered by the Prosecution. This is what we are trying to make you address. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon. In our view the issue of intercept witnesses at this stage is primarily an issue that should be dealt by the Prosecution. It's their case, these are their witnesses. A number of witnesses they intend to bring here is solely in the discretion of the OTP, so there is very little we can do as a defence about it. Its up to the Trial Chamber whether they will allow all these witnesses to come to give their testimony here. On the other hand, and now I am speaking only on behalf of Mr. Borovcanin's defence, we tried very, very hard to avoid any repetitive questions and, if I am not terribly wrong, we -- all our -- all our cross-examination lasted less than 30 minutes. I believe we can do a little bit more of it. In particular, that this issue is not of primary interest of Mr. Borovcanin, since, according to what the Prosecution said, there is only one particular intercept that is -- well, in their view, important for Mr. Borovcanin, and we will stick to this. And we will continue to do -- to make all the efforts to reduce our cross-examination and not to make any repetitive questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau would you like to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we are not receiving interpretation. Can I ask you to start again, Madam Fauveau, again with my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving? What's wrong? If I could ask the French --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now? We've changed over to another console, excuse me. I will repeat what Ms. Fauveau said, with my apologies from the English booth: "Mr. President and judges I would like to support what my colleagues said, Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Meek in that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add to the list of my colleagues, Mr. Bourgon because I would like to support his arguments in particular. I would also like to say that I fully agree with the Chamber in that you have said that this is a presentation of elements of proof which is lengthy and time consuming. Now, as for the Defence, as long as the Prosecutor, as long as the Prosecutor will, as cross-examination, we are forced to do our cross-examination so I agree the questions might be repetitive but the answers are not. Since we get different answers we will carry on asking the same questions about -- in trying to get the truth in all this or out of all this. Should we carry on this way, I do not know, it is not up to the Defence team to say so, it is up to the Prosecutor, as far as I'm concerned. The Defence of General Miletic would be much happier if more of the witnesses knew more about the procedure that applies to how they intercepted on the conversations rather than the intercepts themselves, which are not that important, especially since the Prosecutor has not identified them. So I don't really see how useful it can be to bring in two operators who intercepted a particular conversation, since these persons in general did not identify all intercepts. They have only done a few of them, and the others are in the file. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour has mentioned the possibility of self-regulation by those of us at the bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have shown quite a lot of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the point I am a little curious about, with respect, is at line 19 -- I beg your pardon, at page 19 of the transcript today, Your Honour said, I quote, "We have fully considered what might or could be done with a view to avoiding the continuation of such problems." It would help me certainly and perhaps others if the Trial Chamber were prepared to tell the parties what sort of enforced regulation the Chamber has in mind, as against self-regulation. Because otherwise, with respect, we are slightly making submissions in a vacuum; we don't know what you have in mind. Before I sit down, could I make one other remark? And that's this: Notwithstanding everything that's been said in relation to the army intercept operators we've heard from, we haven't heard from any MUP intercept operators, and certainly we on behalf of General Gvero, wish to ask them some questions and they of course may have rather different answers in relation to techniques as well as everything else. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just quickly before we break, I imagine. I've probably just concluded my only substantial cross-examination of any intercept operator, so I feel a little bit a stranger at this party. Having observed the evidence unfold, I can guess what you've got in mind, but looking around me there is probably something upwards of three or 400 years experience of criminal trial process in front of you, and if we can't sort it out then it is a very sad state of affairs. I would invite you to hold back from imposing regulations upon the examination of any of these witnesses, whether by the Prosecution or the Defence at this stage. It is likely that we are entering, as it were, a pool of witnesses whose relevance to each of the accused is more pin-pointed and you will see things move on a little closer. And there are ways which we do try to employ, on both sides of the chamber, to ensure that we are economical with the Court's time. You've put down a marker, I can guess where you will go next. I would invite you not to do so at this stage, though not out of any interest on my part, because, despite some time to cross-examining the next witnesses, it's highly unlikely that I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you think it will take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given the subject matter, maybe a minute, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be helpful -- it certainly would be helpful for the Prosecution to know a bit more about what the Defence are challenging. We have heard from the beginning that they are challenging the reliability, the accuracy, the processes. This is what I've worked on for many years. We heard from Mr. Ostojic right before the break that he suggested they were a fabrication, I believe, that there was an authenticity issue here, which is a fairly -- it's new and very radical defence. I believe that's what Mr. Zivanovic just said, these are a fabrication. Now, the evidence of proving they are not a fabrication is similar to evidence of showing what they are, but I -- and I don't intend to -- to reintroduce a lot of new evidence on that, but that -- that's helpful to know that, it's a bit late, the law here should provide them to tell us that earlier. But in any event, as we see Mr. Haynes, he's taking a different approach. If I had an idea of what each Defence was saying, as I think the law requires, we would be able to sculpt our case better, because I don't think we're getting any objections from Mr. Haynes, he seems to be going to the substance of that and I don't see -- and I can get from the other cross-examinations some of the same and I can see the people that are challenging the authenticity, but if I could hear that from the others, we may be able to sculpt our case more. We are struggling right now with how much of the MUP evidence to put on. Clearly we want to put on, based on your rulings, the supervisor, full. I would just as soon not have to put on anybody else fully. But we may want to put -- you may want to hear at least one regular operator to see if it is much difference from their perspective, but that is -- my plan with the MUP is to have here the top guy and maybe one operator and then perhaps go the other two 92 ter, if we can, to try to save time. In any event, I don't have a lot to add to this, but if I could get a better view of where the Defence is coming from, we may be able to sculpt ours. I really do not like the idea of us not being able to ask any questions but I can promise you we try to keep it within a half an hour and even shorter on 92 ter. A lot of these you never ask for 92 bis; where we were fine, they just came in. I don't want to go back into time, but if we have to put them on, I would like to at least to be able to ask a few questions since, when you see the witness, so I can point out problems in their testimony. I would prefer to point out issues and mistakes in the testimony as opposed to sit back and have the cross-examination do that. That's -- but I don't want to spend much of your time doing it because I obviously -- we all feel the same frustrations. So that's just my viewpoint on the no comments, no questions. But otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. We will have a 25-minute break. And we will come back to you on this either later on today or tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. One thing. You had mentioned yesterday you wanted us to be able to argue about the -- the other intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we put that off until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I got --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you. I got the impression before we started the sitting that you sent over a message that you would like this to be discussed later on in the day today rather than first thing before we started or something like that. I mean, that's why I didn't raise the matter, that's why I didn't raise the matter in the beginning of the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I got the message. Mr. Bourgon is in the position to make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At any time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was some kind of agreement that it will not be not before, not in the first part of today's sitting, but later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If it at all possible, we could do it tomorrow. Mr. Thayer was the one that was dealing with the subject. I can, of course, deal with it, but I think Mr. Bourgon and I agree it should just happen before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is no problem with the next witness because I, at least, think that you are not going -- or you do not intend to use the intercept with Witness number 81, but only with Witness number 77. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to inform you that I have submitted a motion on yesterday's allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we'll meet again in 25 minutes, 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So on the subject that we were discussing prior to the break, contrary to what some of you may have -- at least that's the impression you gave us, contrary to what you may have thought, we have not yet reached a conclusion on how best to deal with this problem. We are still discussing, and we'll come back to you, as I indicated earlier on, probably tomorrow -- tomorrow morning. If we conclude our deliberations on it. Now, next -- are we agreed that the matter of the intercept, as it relates to 81, we will hear submissions towards the end of this sitting or do you want to make submissions now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are some difficulties associated with this. My colleague, Mr. Zivanovic referred to a motion they filed this morning. This motion is requesting a 14-day delay in order to respond to this issue of the additional intercept. I did have a conversation with my colleague, Mr. McCloskey from the Prosecution. The only where we do agree is this should -- this has to do with whether or not the witness will testify, and we'd like to do those arguments in any event before the witness comes. Whatever the Trial Chamber decides as to when we can argue, I am ready to argue at any time, but with deference to my colleague, maybe another time would be appropriate. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, now, that we have Mr. Zivanovic involved, I -- this witness can be called and can be put on, it will be 92 ter, it will be a summary, he will identify his intercepts and, in fact, he only has two and the one goes to the acts or conduct. He doesn't need to talk about it much, if at all, if that's some -- prejudicial in some way. And the decision can be made after that or sorry the argument can be made after that. I don't see that as crucial. I think it's ideal to have it beforehand, but with the other -- the other position, it's -- it's hard to see how we do that unless we send him home and bring him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I must disagree with my colleague, Mr. President. The witness that we are referring to was initially put and called as a witness on the basis of 21 different intercepts, or 22. We have been informed this morning that out of the 22 intercepts, 20 of those are not his, and therefore they will not be introduced with this witness. So what we are dealing with is one witness with two intercepts left. One of which does not go to the acts and conduct of the accused. I think my colleague will agree to that. And the second one is the disputed intercept. Our point of view, Mr. President, is the this the perfect -- the ideal opportunity simply to say this witness does not need to come because this intercept was added in addition to all the problems that I can relate to as to why this intercept should not be going into evidence, there is no need for this witness to come in the first place. That's why for us, it is important to have this argument before the witness is called and not after, as my colleague suggests. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further submissions on this? All right. We'll come back to you on this later. Anything you wish to state before we bring in witness number 81, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, just to let you know, we have -- yes, this next witness, and -- and the subject witness, and that's all we have for this week, based on the timing. So just to let you know for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Zivanovic, one question to you which would possibly help us see better your -- understand better your request or your motion. In one part of your motion you do accept or at least you don't deny that this intercept has been available for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am not denying that. I am aware of that when -- I was aware of that when I acquainted myself with the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you say that the defence of Vujadin Popovic had no time to read and study the OTP submission before the trial? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify, I didn't have the opportunity to read the submission or to really study it. Not the intercept itself, just the submission. The submission itself, besides indicated the reasons of not placing the intercept on the list, the Prosecution embarks on an analysis of some other matters. I mentioned that in my submission. These are alleged ethnic prejudices indicated on the part of my client, according to the intercept, then some evidence which, through this intercept approves the authenticity of all the other intercepts, and I think because of this we require some time in order to be able to respond. Because this is used as an argument to accept or as a good reason to place this intercept on the 65 ter list of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Looking at the rest of your motion, particularly the last two pages, don't you really address the -- the question that was raised by ourselves in the first place, because we only requested the Prosecution to show on a prima facie basis, good cause, why this intercept should be included in the 65 ter, and you are, although you say you haven't had time to familiarise yourself with -- with the submissions of the Prosecution, you address them all, and try to convince the Trial Chamber that they haven't shown good cause for -- for -- so I -- seems to be conflicting statements in -- in the same -- in the same motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I wasn't clear, I will try to go over it again. The submission itself, yesterday, when you put that question at the beginning of the session, at that time I was not familiar with the submission. But the intercept from the 20th of April, 1995, I was familiar with that. I was not familiar with the contents of the submission, especially the reasons which are presented as good reasons, valid reasons, why the Prosecution did not place the intercept earlier on the 65 ter list. The reasons I already mentioned are that in the analysis of the intercept itself, it is stated that my client demonstrates ethnic intolerance and that the intercept allegedly confirms the veracity of all the other intercepts. These are the reasons. I was not aware of these allegations yesterday when it was discussed. Not with the intercept itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you address these issues in your motion. Anyway, let's leave it and we will come to it tomorrow. This next witness, number 81, could someone remind me the protective measures that we have put in place? I know it's pseudonym for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My understanding is that he has protective measures in the form of facial distortion only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Facial distortion only and not voice distortion. All right. There is still the unfinished symphony as far as he is concerned. Namely we are still not yet decided on the Prosecution's request to have him testify as a 92 ter witness. That still has not yet been decided. To my knowledge, as I pointed out yesterday, none of the defence teams have objected to having this witness testify under rule 92 ter. Do I have a confirmation of that? Yeah, I see -- I hear no comments, which I take to be a confirmation of what I said earlier, that there are no objections. So your motion, insofar as this witness is concerned, and namely to present him as a 92 ter witness is hereby being granted orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your motion will then be decided limitedly to the other witness, namely number 77. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are welcome to start giving evidence. Our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath. In some jurisdictions that in the course of your testimony, that you will be speaking the truth. The text is being handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please read that out and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Make yourself comfortable, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have put in place for you some protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym instead of your name, and also face distortion. In other words no one will be able to see your face outside the four walls of this courtroom. We have a distorted image. I think this has already been explained to you in full. All I want to know is whether it is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vanderpuye will go first, and he will then be followed by various cross-examinations from the Defence teams. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have P 02346 shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, please have a look at that document and without telling us what is on it, can you confirm whether or not you were the person named on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you some questions in relation to your testimony today, and I would ask that you allow a pause for the purposes of translation before you give your answer. And try to keep your voice up so that the interpreters can hear you. Witness, do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor dated 17th November 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the statement that you gave truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read your statement before having come here to testify today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you read your statement in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the language in which you originally gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you just say what language that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And after having read the statement, are you satisfied that the statement was correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the statement, as you read it, fairly and accurately reflect what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say, were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to read 92 ter summary into the record. The witness completed electro- -- well, may I go into private session for at least the first two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indeed we will do that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.
